newsitem.title: USA: ANALYSIS-Lengthy Fed bias enhances Greenspan role.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS-Lengthy Fed bias enhances Greenspan role.

text.p: The Federal Open Market Committee's decision to maintain a policy bias for an unprecedented seven consecutive months without a rate move enhances the decision-making role of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, Fed watchers said on Wednesday.

"This unprecedented string of tightening biases reflects on greater willingness of FOMC members to confer greater discretion on the Chairman," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International.
The just-released minutes of the December 17 meeting showed the Fed reinstated a bias to tighten credit at a fifth consecutive meeting, covering a period of seven months.
The bias introduced in December was in place until the FOMC convened on Tuesday and Wednesday. The minutes of this week's meeting will be released in late March.

"The unprecedented string of tightening biases shows the chairman has greater flexibility to make policy adjustments," Resler added while noting Greenspan is known for consulting FOMC members via telephone conversations before inter-meeting moves.
The Fed began extensively using a policy bias to notify the New York Fed's Open Market desk of the possibility of an inter-meeting move under the chairmanship of Paul Volcker.

"The bias may have a greater symbolic quality now in the sense the Fed wants to inform the market of the next direction of a rate move rather than of the actual possibility of an inter-meeting move," Resler added.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell managing director Jospeh Carson concurred that "the longest bias in existence under Greenspan is a way of basically saying their next move in rates is not going to be down but up."
Carson also wondered about the new schedule to release the FOMC minutes. The minutes, previously released on late Friday afternoon, are now set for release on Thursday at 2 p.m.

"They released the minutes of this meeting early today to send a message to the market. A cynic would say they released it now for a reason, because there is some information there they want the market to know about," said Carson, who noted the market got the latest news on the Fed's thinking right before the January employment report set for release Friday at 0830 EST/1230 GMT.
Carson further noted the length of time with a tightening bias "indicates their concern about the labor markets."
Ken Bercuson, head of research at SBC Warburg, said the FOMC "is now using the bias in a way that it was not intended to be."

"They are using it to tell the market that if they were going to move, the direction is more likely to be a tightening than an easing," Bercuson noted. "They are looking at the labor markets but they think an upward spike in labor costs will be passed on slowly because of competition."

Bercuson also noted the absence of rate hikes in an environment of strong growth and tight labor markets shows that the Fed does not know where the NAIRU (non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) is.
"They are even not sure to the degree to which wages will be rising given the gap between a given unemployment rate and NAIRU," the SBC Warburg economist said.
